title: Only 30% of secondary teachers trained in health education, study finds
excerpt: A government situation analysis supported by UNESCO finds gaps in teacher training, school health services and the curriculum in Bangladesh's secondary schools.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration for the story: Only 30% of secondary teachers trained in health education, study finds

content:
Fewer than a third of secondary school teachers surveyed in Bangladesh have had any training in health education or well-being, according to a government study of the Health Promoting Schools Programme.

At a glance

  • Title: Situation Analysis Report on the Health Promoting Schools Programme in Bangladesh
  • Published by: Directorate of Secondary and Higher Education (DSHE), Ministry of Education, with support from UNESCO. The programme is implemented by DSHE and the National Academy for Education Management (NAEM).
  • Published: July 2026
  • Method: survey of 458 students and 206 teachers in 48 secondary schools across all eight divisions, plus 24 focus groups, 12 interviews and a review of policy, curriculum and textbooks

Main findings

  • Teacher training is thin. Only 30.1% of surveyed teachers had received health education or well-being training. Rates were lower among teachers in government and rural schools, and training was often short.
  • Policy awareness is low. Many teachers were unfamiliar with national school health provisions.
  • Habits are ahead of knowledge. Students reported many healthy practices, but their overall health knowledge was rated poor.
  • Services vary by school type. Students in non-government schools were more likely to report clean toilets, safe drinking water, anti-bullying measures and a dedicated health worker.
  • Check-ups are not routine. Regular health check-ups were not standard for many students, and arrangements for responding to accidents were not consistently reported.
  • Families are supportive. Nearly 93% of students said their parents encourage healthy practices at home.
  • Curriculum gaps. Road safety, drug and suicide prevention, emergency response, environmental health, and menstrual and reproductive health need more attention.

Limitation: the findings on school facilities reflect what students reported, not physical inspections.

What the report recommends

  • Better coordination among the education, health, youth and sports, women and children affairs, and social welfare ministries
  • More teacher training, including first aid
  • Referral links between schools and local health facilities
  • Improved sanitation and nutrition in schools
  • Qualified physical education teachers and regular physical activity
  • Dedicated financing for school health

Why it matters

The report gives NGOs working on school health, WASH in schools, adolescent health and education a clear, government-owned list of gaps to plan around. Teacher training and school sanitation are areas where NGO programmes and donor funding can directly support the recommendations.
